text: Farrukh ibn Hasan al-Nishapuri had lived nineteen years without once hearing his father's own name spoken aloud. To the bazaar, to the mosque, to the tax-farmer's clerks, the man who raised him was {{khwaja,kunya|Khwaja Abu Farrukh}} - "master, father of Farrukh" - and that was enough of a name for a man to die under.

text: It was a bad season to be caught grieving. Riders had come through the Chahar Su market three weeks running with the same unsettling murmur - Turkmen horsemen loose again on the Khorasan frontier, a garrison broken somewhere near {{nasa|Nasa}}, word passed caravan to caravan faster than any courier the Sultan employed. Farrukh had barely marked it. His father's cough had turned to fever on the same week the news arrived, as if the sickness in the empire's far edge had found its way, by some private road, into one merchant's chest in Ghazni.

choices.text: Continue.

text: He died on a Thursday. His body was washed that same afternoon by his brother and two men from the mosque - {{ghusl|ghusl}}, three times over, the last water scented with camphor - and wrapped before evening in plain white cloth, three lengths of it, unmarked, unadorned. Farrukh had expected - he did not know what he had expected. Not this. Not a shroud identical, thread for thread, to the one they'd have wrapped a beggar in behind the grain market. {{kafan|Kafan}} made no distinction. That was the point of it, someone told him gently. He did not feel comforted.

text: At the grave they said the {{janaza|janaza}} standing, no bowing, near-silent - and it was there, in front of half the merchants of the western bazaar, that the trouble surfaced into the open air. The imam did not begin. He turned, instead, to the men close by, and asked, plainly, the question the Prophet himself was remembered to have asked before he would pray over a man: is he in debt? Someone answered before Farrukh could. Yes. Considerably. To two houses, maybe three. Nobody was certain how much, because nobody - not his mother, not the clerks, not the dead man's own partner - had yet opened the ledger. The imam did not move to pray.

choices.text: Step forward now, before anyone else decides for him.
Wait - let an elder answer first.

text: Nobody among the assembled {{tajir|tajirs}} had stepped forward yet. Farrukh did not wait for one of them to. He was already moving before the silence had finished settling over the grave.

choices.text: Continue.

text: He waited one breath, then two, watching the older, richer men of the bazaar find reasons not to meet the imam's eyes. Nobody stepped forward. So Farrukh did.

choices.text: Continue.

text: He said the words before he had decided to say them, the way a man's hand moves before his mind has finished arguing with it: that he would stand for his father's debt himself - all of it, whatever it proved to be - {{kafala|damān}}, his word as guarantee, in front of every man there to remember it. It was not required of him. No qadi, no creditor, no verse of the Book would have compelled a son to answer for a father's failed venture beyond whatever the estate itself could cover - a fact he did not yet know, and that would have changed nothing if he had. He said it because the alternative was standing silent while his father was refused a grave.

text: The imam prayed. Grief afterward observed its three days of {{taziya|ta'ziya}} - visitors, murmured {{rahimahu_llah|rahimahu llah}}, trays of food from neighbors Farrukh could not later remember thanking. His mother sat through all three days at the head of the room, taking each condolence with a stillness Farrukh recognized as his own, inherited from somewhere he'd never thought to ask - and once, on the second evening, when the room had briefly emptied, reached over and gripped his wrist hard enough to hurt, said nothing, and let go.

text: It was on the second of those three days that Nasuh - his father's old clerk, a quiet, ink-stained man who had kept the shop's accounts for eleven years - finally opened the ledger in front of him, and went very still reading it. The debts were real, and worse than the bazaar's rumor. But it was not the sums that troubled Nasuh. It was a {{suftaja|suftaja}} from a banking house in Rayy that Farrukh's father had never mentioned owning, promising a payment against goods that, by the manifest, did not match anything the shop had ever carried west - and a second paper, unsigned, in a hand Nasuh did not recognize, that used a word for the shipment's origin that made the old clerk fold it shut before Farrukh could finish reading it.

text: "Some accounts," Nasuh said, "are better settled on the road than argued over in this house." His hand stayed on the folded paper. He had not put it away yet.

choices.text: Ask to see the letter in full before it's put away.
Let Nasuh fold it away. Ask no more tonight.

text: Nasuh unfolded it again, reluctant, and Farrukh read it through to the end. He understood perhaps a third of it - enough to know the word that had stopped Nasuh cold was not a word either of them should be saying aloud in a house still receiving condolence visitors.

choices.text: Continue.

text: Nasuh folded it away without another word, visibly relieved not to have to say the word out loud a second time. Farrukh let him. There would be time on the road, he told himself, not quite believing it.

choices.text: Continue.

text: That night, an old friend of his father's - a traveling letter-writer who called himself nothing grander than {{ostad|ostad}}, though he had read further than most qadis - sat with Farrukh outside the shuttered shop and offered the only comfort that didn't feel like a lie. They say the physicians in the west - Bukhara once, Hamadan after, Isfahan now, safe in some Kakuyid prince's service and well out of any Sultan's reach these days - argue that a man stripped of every sense, every last touch of his own skin, would still know one thing for certain: that he is. That the self isn't the body at all. "Whatever's under that shroud," the old man said, "was never the whole of your father. Only what could be borrowed. The rest went somewhere law and ledgers don't reach."

choices.text: Let it be a comfort, and say nothing.
Tell him you would rather have the body than the argument.

text: Nasuh found him alone that last morning, before the household had properly woken, and pressed something into his hands without much ceremony - a ledger, blank, its covers not yet broken in. "You'll want your own accounts, out there," he said, in the same flat voice he used for tallying debts, though his eyes didn't quite match the flatness. "Your father kept his in a hand I could read blind after eleven years. I don't imagine yours will look anything like it. Keep it anyway." He did not say what he meant by that, and Farrukh did not ask him to.

text: His mother did not come to see him off with the others gathering in the yard. She found him alone at the door instead, and said nothing at all - the same silence she'd kept through three days of visitors, the same stillness he'd felt in her grip on the second evening of ta'ziya. She took his hand, turned it palm-up, and set something small and cold into it: a seal-stamp, old, worn smooth at the edges, marked with a device that belonged to no house Farrukh had ever seen his father deal with. She closed his fingers over it herself, the way she might have done when he was young enough to need reminding not to drop things, and let go. She had not shown it to Nasuh. She had not shown it to anyone.

text: The village stood a little off the road where the canal came down out of the hills, and Farrukh heard what was wrong with it some while before he saw anything at all. A mill announces itself for a good distance - the paddles, the leat running full, that low grinding a man who has lived over a shop learns to stop hearing by the time he is eight - and this one announced nothing whatever, at an hour of the morning when the wheel of a working mill has no business standing still. His guide, who knew the road past Teginabad and had priced the knowing accordingly, said the place had a name and did not trouble himself to offer it. Nor did any dog come out to argue with the mules, which Farrukh noticed only after he had been listening for one for some time; a village answers a caravan with dogs, always, and this one let them come up along the wall and past it in silence. There was smoke off three roofs out of a dozen, and it was thin smoke, dung rather than wood. The threshing floor by the road had been swept bare in a season when a threshing floor ought to be knee deep in chaff. And one door on the lane, the nearest one, stood tied shut with a length of cord on the outside of it, knotted twice, by somebody who had then walked away from it.

choices.text: Sickness. They have shut themselves in and are waiting it out.
Nobody is shut in there. They are leaving, a few households at a time.

text: He came up on them where the road bent around a walled garden gone to seed: a man about the age his father had got to, a wife, a grown daughter, two boys, and a handcart pushed by two of them and steered by the third at the shaft. What was in the cart was iron, mostly - the spindle out of a mill, the iron shoe off the bed stone, a hand quern with one handle left on it - which is what a family takes away when the thing it is leaving cannot be carried and cannot be sold to anybody who will still be there to use it. The water share had been read out again in the spring. Lawfully, the man said: an order with a seal on it and the water master to say the words aloud, and the head of their leat going now to broken ground newly put under plough by a household that had standing where they had none. He recited the whole of it in the flat voice of a man who has lost the argument already and keeps the words by him anyway. They still had the old grant. He carried it in a fold of his sleeve, wrapped in rag against the sweat, and brought it out to show Farrukh that they were not people who walked a road without papers, and held it upside down the entire time he was showing it.

text: The grant said what they had hoped it said, which was the half of it he could give them, and said nothing whatever about a later order lawfully made, which was the half he had to give them as well. The eldest took both halves standing, and then asked for the other thing, badly, having plainly been working at how to put it the whole time Farrukh was reading. A line on the back of the grant. In a merchant's hand, with a merchant's name under the line, saying only this: that the mill made no sound at all, at an hour when a working mill is heard from the road, on the morning the merchant went by. Not that the wheel had stopped, which the man pointed out himself, since a stranger passing on the far side of a wall could not swear to a wheel he had never laid eyes on - only the silence, which was a thing a passing stranger did have. At Teginabad, he explained, a paper with somebody else's hand on it gets read; a paper with only their own goes on the pile to be read afterwards, if an afterwards comes. Farrukh had the ledger Nasuh had pressed on him and the ink to go with it, and understood the shape of what was wanted: no lie in it anywhere, nothing he had not heard with his own two ears, and his own name written into another district's quarrel in a town where his own load had yet to be declared.

text_variants.text: Having had the grant read out to them without anybody having to ask whether he had letters, they came at the next thing as though it followed from the first, which for them it did, and which was the difficulty. The eldest did not work up to it. He turned the paper over while Farrukh was still holding it, put a thumb on the clean back of it and said what he wanted written there: that the mill made no sound at all, at an hour when a working mill is heard from the road, on the morning the merchant went by. Not that the wheel had stopped, since a man on the far side of a wall cannot swear to a wheel he never laid eyes on - only the silence, which he did have. He set that limit out himself, easily, in the manner of a man who has stopped expecting to be refused. At Teginabad, he explained, a paper with another hand on it gets read; a paper with only their own goes on the pile. Farrukh had the ledger Nasuh had pressed on him and the ink to go with it. He had also established, at no cost to himself and inside a quarter of an hour, that he was a man who does things before he is asked, which is a poor position from which to explain that his hand is not his to lend to another district's quarrel in a town where his own load has yet to be declared.

choices.text: Write the line, and put your name under it.

text: Where the road came down to cross the line of the canal there was a clerk working the line the other way, a boy leading his donkey and a board under his arm with a ruled sheet pinned to it, and he came down off the bank to stop the caravan with the mild, unhurried authority of a man who does this to everybody and has never in his life had to raise his voice about it. Origin, load, where bound. Then whether they had passed anyone on the road with a cart, and how many were walking with it, and out of which village. That last was not idleness. A district is assessed on the district, and every household that walks out of one leaves its share standing there to be made up by the households that stayed, so the clerk went along the line counting the ones who had gone, so that they might be found later and the share carried forward against them, which was tedious and lawful and would go on being both for years. The boy held the donkey and looked at the mules. Farrukh had passed people on this road that morning, and saying so would take him the better part of one breath and cost him nothing at all, which was, with the question sitting out in the open between them, precisely the trouble with it.

text_variants.text: Where the road came down to cross the line of the canal there was a clerk working the line the other way, a boy leading his donkey and a board under his arm with a ruled sheet pinned to it, and he came down off the bank with the mild, unhurried authority of a man who does this to everybody and has never had to raise his voice about it. Origin, load, where bound. Then whether they had passed anyone on the road with a cart, and how many were walking with it, and out of which village. A district is assessed on the district, and the households that stay make up whatever the households that left do not, so the line gets walked and the ones who have gone get counted, and found later, and charged, which is tedious and lawful and will go on being both for years. The difficulty was no longer whether Farrukh had passed anybody. He had stood in the road with their grant open in his hands and read it out to them, in front of his own guide, in front of two mule boys who would be drinking in Teginabad by tomorrow night, and in front of a family who would give an honest account of their morning to the next man entitled to ask them for one, and who would remember the merchant kindly, and by name if they had thought to ask for it. Saying nothing would still cost him one breath. It would no longer cost him nothing.

choices.text: Tell him that what is behind you is not on your manifest.
Tell him who you passed. It is what he is asking.

text: Farrukh did not know if he believed it. He packed the shop's remaining goods into two mules' worth of load, hired a caravan guide who knew the road past Teginabad, and set out from Ghazni's western gate before the week's mourning was fully spent - a blank ledger and an unmarked seal riding in his pack alongside whatever else he'd thought worth taking - toward Nishapur, toward whatever his father had actually been carrying, and toward a frontier that the riders from Nasa said was already starting to come apart. The first night on the road felt less like grief than like its absence - no house creaking with half-recognized relatives, no incense still burning for a man not yet a fortnight dead, only the guide's fire, the mules stamping at nothing in particular, and a silence so total after Ghazni's noise that it took him most of the night to understand it wasn't unfriendly, just indifferent. He had expected the road to feel like running from something. Instead it felt, for these first few hours at least, like the first honest quiet he'd had since his father died - the kind a house full of mourners never once let him keep.
